prompt: A delivery time sits at the 80th percentile. What does that mean?
hint: What share of the data is at or below it?

choices.text: It took 80 minutes
choices.why: A percentile is a position in the data, not a number of minutes.

choices.text: It is 80% slower than the mean
choices.why: Percentiles say nothing about distance from the mean, only about order.

choices.text: 80% took that long or less
choices.why: Right. The pth percentile has p% of the data at or below it.

choices.text: It was faster than 80% of deliveries
choices.why: The reverse: 80% were as fast or faster, so this one is among the slower fifth.

prompt: Horta wants to promise a delivery time that customers can rely on. Why is a high percentile better for that than the mean?

choices.text: Percentiles are easier to compute
choices.why: Ease is not the point, and a percentile involves sorting and interpolation.

choices.text: It says how slow things get for nearly everyone
choices.why: Right. A promise is judged by the slow cases, and a high percentile describes exactly those.

choices.text: The mean includes outliers, which are errors
choices.why: Slow deliveries are real, and they are what the promise must cover.

choices.text: A percentile is never affected by the data
choices.why: A percentile comes from the data like any summary.

prompt: Using PERCENTILE.INC's rule, what is the 75th percentile of 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50?
Using the spreadsheet's QUARTILE.INC rule, what is Q1 of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10?
Your Q1 for a column is 32.625 and a colleague's is 32.25, from the same twelve values. What is the most likely explanation?
hint: How many correct ways are there to compute a quartile?

choices.text: One of you made an arithmetic mistake
choices.why: Possible, but the two numbers are exactly what two correct methods give on Horta's data.

choices.text: Two different quartile rules
choices.why: Right. QUARTILE.INC gives 32.625 and the median-of-halves hand method gives 32.25; both are correct.

choices.text: The data was sorted differently
choices.why: Sorted data has one order; it cannot be sorted two ways.

choices.text: Quartiles change each time they are computed
choices.why: Each method is deterministic; the same rule gives the same answer every time.

prompt: The second quartile, Q2, is another name for the ___.
hint: Half the data on each side.

prompt: Q1 is 42.56 and Q3 is 106.38. What is the IQR? Give two decimal places.
The slowest of the twelve deliveries is retyped as 610 minutes instead of 61. What happens to the standard deviation and the IQR?
hint: Which of the two uses the size of the slowest value?

choices.text: The standard deviation soars; the IQR stays
choices.why: Right. The IQR ignores the top quarter, so one wild value cannot reach it. The standard deviation grows to over 160.

choices.text: Both grow by about the same amount
choices.why: The IQR does not move at all; only the standard deviation uses that value's size.

choices.text: The IQR grows; the standard deviation stays, being robust
choices.why: It is the other way round: the IQR is the robust one.

choices.text: Neither changes, because only one value moved
choices.why: One value is all it takes to move the standard deviation, whose breakdown point is a single value.

prompt: A report gives a median with a standard deviation for skewed basket data. What is the problem?
hint: Which spread is robust, like the median?

choices.text: A median and a standard deviation cannot both be computed on the same data
choices.why: Both can be computed; the trouble is what pairing them says.

choices.text: The standard deviation of money is meaningless
choices.why: Money is on a ratio scale, where a standard deviation is allowed.

choices.text: Skewed data has no median
choices.why: Every numerical data set has a median.

choices.text: It mixes a robust centre with a spread pulled by the tail
choices.why: Right. Report the median with the IQR, or the mean with the standard deviation.

prompt: Q1 is 20 and Q3 is 30. By the 1.5 IQR rule, above what value is a point beyond the upper fence?
Put the five-number summary in order, from smallest to largest.
hint: Each one cuts off a further quarter.

prompt: A five-number summary reads 10, 40, 45, 50, 60. Which way is the data skewed?
hint: Compare the gaps on the left with those on the right.

choices.text: To the right: the maximum is far from the median
choices.why: The maximum is 15 above the median, but the minimum is 35 below it; the long side is the left.

choices.text: To the left: the bottom quarter is widest
choices.why: Right. The gap from the minimum to Q1 is 30, against 10 from Q3 to the maximum.

choices.text: Neither: the box is symmetric, so the data is
choices.why: The box is symmetric, but the whiskers are not, and the tails are part of the shape.

choices.text: It cannot be told without the mean
choices.why: The gaps between the five numbers describe the shape on their own.

prompt: In a boxplot, what does the length of the box show?
hint: Where does the box start and end?

choices.text: The range of the data
choices.why: The range runs from end to end, whiskers and points included.

choices.text: Two standard deviations, one each side of the mean
choices.why: A boxplot is built from quartiles, not from the mean and the standard deviation.

choices.text: The IQR
choices.why: Right. The box runs from Q1 to Q3 and holds the middle half of the data.

choices.text: How many values are in the data
choices.why: A boxplot does not show the count; that is one of the things it hides.

prompt: A boxplot's right whisker is three times as long as its left, and the median sits near the left end of the box. What does that say?
hint: Same count in each part; what does a longer part mean?

choices.text: The data has a tail on the left
choices.why: A left tail would make the left whisker long and push the median right.

choices.text: There is a tail on the right
choices.why: Right. The upper values are more spread out than the lower ones, both inside the box and beyond it.

choices.text: The right whisker contains more values
choices.why: Each whisker covers about a quarter of the data; length shows spread, not count.

choices.text: The values on the right are errors
choices.why: A long whisker is a shape, not a verdict about errors.

prompt: Seventeen of the 400 baskets are drawn as separate points beyond the right whisker. What should Horta conclude?
hint: Is the rule a verdict or a pointer?

choices.text: Seventeen orders were recorded wrongly
choices.why: The rule flags values for a look; in long-tailed money data it flags plenty of real orders.

choices.text: The 1.5 IQR rule has failed and should be ignored
choices.why: The rule did its job, which is to point at the unusual values, not to judge them.

choices.text: The boxplot shows the data is bimodal
choices.why: A boxplot cannot show two peaks; it hides them.

choices.text: They deserve a look; big baskets are plausible
choices.why: Right. Points beyond the fence are where to look, and a monthly shop of R$ 300 is a real order until shown otherwise.

prompt: Match each part of a boxplot to what it marks.
hint: Tukey's boxplot uses quartiles and one rule.

pairs.left: the two ends of the box

pairs.right: the most extreme value within 1.5 IQR
a value beyond 1.5 IQR from the box

prompt: In the four neighbourhood boxplots, Barão Geraldo's box does not overlap any other. What does that suggest?
hint: Where is Barão Geraldo's Q1 compared with the others' Q3?

choices.text: Barão Geraldo's data is wrong
choices.why: Far-away deliveries taking longer is exactly what you would expect.

choices.text: The four neighbourhoods have the same typical time
choices.why: Non-overlapping boxes say the opposite.

choices.text: Its deliveries are clearly slower than the others
choices.why: Right. Even its fastest quarter is slower than three quarters of every other neighbourhood's deliveries.

choices.text: It has more outliers than the others
choices.why: It has none in this data; position, not outliers, is what separates it.

prompt: Why are side-by-side boxplots better than a bar chart of the four mean delivery times?
hint: What does a single bar per group leave out?

choices.text: They show spread and stragglers as well as the centre
choices.why: Right. A bar of means hides that Barão Geraldo is less predictable and that Centro has a straggler.

choices.text: Means cannot be compared across groups
choices.why: They can be compared; they just leave out most of each distribution.

choices.text: Bar charts are only for categorical data, and time is numerical
choices.why: A bar of means per category is a legitimate chart; it is just less informative.

choices.text: Boxplots prove which differences are real
choices.why: Boxplots show differences; testing them is lesson 16's job.
